I think you may mean **Dorie Miller** — whose full name was **Doris “Dorie” Miller** — the famous African American U.S. Navy hero from World War II. If you meant a different **Doris K. Miller**, let me know and I’ll look at that person instead.

## Doris “Dorie” Miller at a glance
- **Born:** October 12, 1919, in **Waco, Texas**
- **Died:** November 24, 1943, in the **Pacific Theater** during World War II
- **Known for:** Heroism during the **Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor** on December 7, 1941
- **Branch:** U.S. Navy
- **Rank:** **Mess Att Attendant, Third Class** at the time of Pearl Harbor
- **Legacy:** One of the most celebrated Black heroes of World War II; later recognized by multiple ships, monuments, and honors

## Early life
Dorie Miller was born into a large African American family in Texas. He grew up during the era of segregation and limited opportunities for Black Americans. He attended school in Waco and was known as a strong athlete, especially in football.

Before joining the Navy, he worked a variety of jobs, including as a cook and laborer. Like many Black men of his era, he entered military service in a segregated system that restricted many roles for African Americans.

## Navy service before Pearl Harbor
Miller enlisted in the U.S. Navy in 1939. Because of Navy racial policies at the time, Black sailors were generally limited to service roles such as mess attendant or steward rather than combat assignments.

He served aboard several ships before being assigned to the **USS West Virginia** (BB-48), a battleship stationed at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii.

## Heroism at Pearl Harbor
On the morning of **December 7, 1941**, Japan attacked Pearl Harbor. Miller was on board the **USS West Virginia** when the attack began.

His actions during the attack made him famous:

- He helped carry wounded sailors to safety.
- He was ordered to assist the ship’s anti-aircraft battery.
- Although he had **no formal gunnery training**, he manned a .50-caliber machine gun and fired at attacking Japanese planes.
- He continued helping the crew until he was ordered to abandon ship.

Reports of his exact number of planes hit vary and are hard to verify, but what mattered was that he acted courageously under fire, in a situation where Black sailors were not expected to be placed in such roles.

## Recognition and awards
Miller became one of the first major American heroes of World War II, especially significant because he was a Black serviceman recognized for combat bravery during an era of widespread segregation.

He was awarded:
- The **Navy Cross** in 1942, one of the U.S. Navy’s highest decorations for valor

At the time, this was a very significant recognition for a Black sailor. The award citation praised his bravery during the Pearl Harbor attack.

## Later service and death
After Pearl Harbor, Miller was promoted and eventually assigned to the escort carrier **USS Liscome Bay**.

He died on **November 24, 1943**, when the **USS Liscome Bay** was torpedoed and sunk during the Battle of Makin in the Gilbert Islands campaign.

He was only 24 years old.

## Why he matters historically
Dorie Miller’s importance goes beyond one battle.

### 1. He became a symbol of Black patriotism and courage
At a time when African Americans faced segregation in the military and society, Miller’s heroism challenged racist assumptions about who could serve bravely in combat.

### 2. He helped pressure the military toward change
His fame was part of the broader momentum that eventually pushed the U.S. military toward greater integration, although full desegregation would not come until later, under President Truman in 1948.

### 3. He became a national role model
He was honored in Black newspapers, by civil rights leaders, and in popular memory as a symbol of dignity, bravery, and competence.

## Honors and legacy
Dorie Miller’s name has been honored in many ways over the decades, including:

- **USS Miller (DE-1091)**, a frigate named in his honor
- **Doris Miller Hall** and other buildings/schools named after him
- Statues, plaques, and memorials
- Ongoing efforts to recognize him in broader American history

In 2020, there was also a major campaign to name a future U.S. Navy aircraft carrier after him. That effort was widely reported and sparked discussion about how the Navy commemorates its heroes.

## Interesting facts
- “Dorie” was a nickname; his first name was **Doris**.
- He was not a trained gunner, which makes his actions at Pearl Harbor even more remarkable.
- He was one of the first Black Americans to receive the Navy Cross.
- His story became especially important because it highlighted both heroism and racial injustice in the WWII-era military.

## In one sentence
**Doris “Dorie” Miller was a Black U.S. Navy sailor and World War II hero best known for his bravery during the attack on Pearl Harbor, where he manned anti-aircraft guns under fire and later received the Navy Cross.**
